stem: During intake, collegiate sprinter Temitope Ibekwe completes the CSAI-2 before a conference meet. Her cognitive and somatic anxiety intensity scores are well above her team's average, yet her coach notes she has run personal bests at nearly every high-stakes meet this season. Temitope asks whether her nerves are a problem. Drawing on Jones's directional perspective on competitive anxiety, what additional information would most help the consultant interpret her scores?
options: How her current intensity scores compare with her ratings before past best and worst meets
Whether her worry builds earlier in race week than her physical symptoms do
Whether she sees each of her symptoms as helping or hindering her sprinting
How her intensity scores compare with published norms for collegiate sprinters
rationales: Comparing current emotions with those before best and worst performances is the idiographic method of the IZOF model. It is a sound approach, but it still measures intensity and does not tell the consultant how she reads her symptoms, which is the question the directional perspective raises.

The timing of cognitive versus somatic anxiety is a prediction of multidimensional anxiety theory. Knowing when each component rises would help with scheduling strategies, but it does not explain why high intensity accompanies her best races.

Jones's directional perspective holds that the same intensity of anxiety can be interpreted as facilitative or debilitative, and direction often explains performance better than intensity. Her strong results despite high intensity suggest she may read her symptoms as helpful, which only a direction rating can confirm.
Normative comparisons describe how much anxiety she reports relative to others, which is intensity information the consultant already has; norms cannot reveal how she interprets those symptoms.
takeaway: When anxiety intensity and performance don't line up, assess direction: is the athlete reading the symptoms as facilitative or debilitative?

stem: Tomasz Wierzbicki, an elite single sculler, wants to understand how his emotional state before races relates to how he performs. He says some of his best races came when he felt wound up and others when he felt calm, and he is unsure what to aim for. The consultant decides to plan the assessment around Hanin's IZOF model. Which assessment approach best fits that model?
options: Have him rate the emotions he recalls feeling before several of his best and worst races
Give him the CSAI-2 before each race and compare his scores with elite-rower norms
Rate his arousal before each race and track whether his results peak at moderate levels
Have him rate whether his pre-race symptoms feel facilitative or debilitative each time
rationales: IZOF holds that each athlete has a personal zone of optimal emotional intensity and content, so assessment starts with the individual: retrospective ratings of emotions before best and worst performances (later checked against ratings before actual races) identify his own optimal and dysfunctional zones.
IZOF rejects group norms as the standard, because an intensity that is too high for one rower may be optimal for another; a normative comparison cannot locate his personal zone.

Testing for a moderate-arousal peak applies the inverted-U hypothesis; IZOF predicts that an athlete's optimal zone can sit at low, moderate, or high intensity and includes the content of emotions, not just arousal level.

Rating facilitative versus debilitative direction applies Jones's directional perspective. It adds useful information about interpretation, but it does not map the specific emotions and intensities that make up his individual optimal zone.
takeaway: IZOF assessment is idiographic: identify the athlete's own best-performance emotional zone from his history, not from norms or a universal moderate target.

stem: The artistic director of a pre-professional ballet company asks a consultant to find out why several talented teenage dancers seem anxious and are talking about leaving, and whether company practices are part of the problem. The director posts weekly casting rankings and praises dancers mainly when they outshine their peers. The consultant already plans to measure each dancer's task and ego goal orientation. Grounded in achievement goal theory, what else should the assessment capture?
options: Each dancer's perceived ability relative to peers, since low perceived ability heightens risk
Each dancer's competitive trait anxiety, to see who is most prone to worry about casting
Each dancer's reasons for dancing, placed along the self-determination continuum
Dancers' perceptions of what the company values and rewards in class and rehearsal
rationales: Perceived ability is part of achievement goal theory and matters for ego-oriented dancers, but it is another person-level variable; it cannot show whether the director's practices are shaping the dancers' motivation, which is what the director wants to know.

Trait anxiety is a person-level variable that may be worth knowing, but it overlooks the situational factor achievement goal theory emphasizes, and the stem points to the director's practices as a likely contributor.

Locating dancers on the self-determination continuum applies a different, well-supported theory. It describes the quality of their motivation but is not the environmental construct achievement goal theory pairs with goal orientation.

Achievement goal theory treats motivation as a product of dispositional orientation and the perceived motivational climate. Public rankings and peer-comparison praise suggest an ego-involving (performance) climate, so measuring how dancers perceive what the company emphasizes is essential to judge the company's role in their anxiety and dropout talk.
takeaway: Achievement goal theory directs assessment at both the person (task/ego orientation) and the environment (perceived mastery vs. performance climate).

stem: Collegiate golfer Diego Fuentes completes the CSAI-2 before several tournaments. His results show consistently high cognitive anxiety, moderate somatic anxiety, and high self-confidence, and his scores on the course have worsened as his worry has increased. According to multidimensional anxiety theory, which finding should the consultant treat as the priority when building his plan?
options: His somatic anxiety, since the theory predicts an inverted-U and he may be drifting past its peak
His cognitive anxiety, since the theory links rising worry to steadily poorer performance
His self-confidence, since the theory predicts that further gains will lift his scores in a linear way
The interaction of worry and arousal, since high worry can make rising arousal cause a sudden drop
rationales: The theory does predict an inverted-U for somatic anxiety, but his somatic anxiety is moderate, close to the predicted optimum, and his decline tracks his worry rather than his bodily symptoms.

Multidimensional anxiety theory predicts a negative linear relationship between cognitive anxiety and performance. Diego's high worry, tracking his worsening scores, is the component the theory flags as most harmful, so it should be the plan's first target.
The theory does predict a positive linear relationship between self-confidence and performance, but his confidence is already high; it is a strength to protect, not the component driving his decline.

An interaction in which high worry turns rising arousal into a sudden collapse is the catastrophe model, not multidimensional anxiety theory, and his data show a steady decline with worry rather than an abrupt drop.
takeaway: Multidimensional anxiety theory: cognitive anxiety lowers performance linearly, somatic anxiety follows an inverted-U, and self-confidence raises performance linearly.

stem: A consultant reviews a season of data from professional basketball player Keisha Morrow: pre-game worry ratings, warm-up heart rate, and free-throw percentage. When her worry was low, her shooting changed only gradually as heart rate rose. When her worry was high, her shooting held steady as heart rate rose and then dropped off abruptly. Which model best accounts for this pattern?
options: The inverted-U hypothesis
Multidimensional anxiety theory
Individual zones of optimal functioning
The catastrophe model
rationales: The inverted-U hypothesis predicts a smooth, symmetrical rise and fall of performance with arousal and has no role for cognitive anxiety, so it cannot explain why the abrupt drop appears only when worry is high.

Multidimensional anxiety theory separates cognitive and somatic anxiety, but it predicts independent effects (a linear decline with worry, an inverted-U for somatic anxiety) rather than an interaction that produces a sudden collapse.

IZOF describes athletes' personal optimal zones of emotional intensity, but it does not specify an interaction in which cognitive anxiety determines whether rising physiological arousal produces a gradual or a sudden change.

Hardy's catastrophe model proposes that cognitive anxiety and physiological arousal interact: with low cognitive anxiety, arousal has a mild inverted-U effect, but with high cognitive anxiety, arousal past a certain point produces a sudden, large performance drop. Keisha's data match that interaction.
takeaway: An abrupt performance collapse as arousal rises, appearing only when worry is high, is the signature of the catastrophe model.

stem: Collegiate rower Kazuki Matsuda tells the consultant, "I keep showing up to 5 a.m. practice because I'd feel ashamed if I quit after everything my family sacrificed." He reports little enjoyment and says he isn't sure rowing matters to him anymore. Using self-determination theory to interpret this, which plan goal is most appropriate?
options: Help him explore whether rowing still connects to goals and values that matter to him
Help him set short-term performance goals so he can see steady progress in the boat
Help him build closer bonds with teammates so early practices feel more enjoyable
Help him explore how gratitude for his family's support can fuel his early practices
rationales: Kazuki describes introjected regulation: he participates to avoid guilt and shame, an internal but controlling form of motivation linked to low enjoyment. Self-determination theory recommends fostering more autonomous regulation (identified or integrated) by helping him find personally valued reasons, which also respects his freedom to decide how rowing fits his life.
Visible progress supports the need for competence, but his problem is the controlling reason he participates; better results would not change why he rows or whether it matters to him.
Closer bonds support relatedness and may make practices more pleasant, but they leave the guilt-based reason for rowing in place and do not address his doubt about whether the sport matters to him.

Framing his family's sacrifices as fuel sounds positive, but it strengthens the obligation-based pressure that defines introjected regulation, which self-determination theory associates with lower well-being and enjoyment.
takeaway: Guilt- or shame-driven participation is introjected regulation; SDT-consistent plans help the athlete find personally endorsed reasons rather than add pressure or meet other needs.

stem: Firefighter recruit Lena Brandt must complete an aerial ladder climb to graduate from the academy. She climbs confidently to the third rung of the training ladder but freezes above it, and she rates her confidence for the full climb as very low. Her instructors can offer several kinds of support in the four weeks before the test. Based on Bandura's self-efficacy theory, which support would give her the strongest source of efficacy information?
options: Watching a classmate with similar fears hesitate at first and then finish the climb
Feedback from a respected instructor explaining why her technique is ready for the test
A series of supervised climbs that start low and rise a few rungs at a time
Training in reading her racing heart and shaky legs as normal signs of readiness
rationales: A similar coping model is the most effective form of vicarious experience, but vicarious information is still weaker than her own success at height.

Credible, specific feedback is the most useful form of verbal persuasion, yet persuasion is generally a weaker and less durable source than direct experience, especially when her own attempts have stalled at the third rung.

Bandura identifies performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) as the most powerful source of self-efficacy. A graded sequence of successful climbs gives her direct evidence that she can do the task at each new height.
Reinterpreting physiological states is a legitimate source of efficacy information, but it does not supply what she most lacks: personal success above the third rung.
takeaway: Among Bandura's sources, graded mastery experiences give the strongest efficacy information; well-chosen models, credible persuasion, and arousal reappraisal support but don't replace them.

stem: After losing three close matches, 15-year-old tennis player Zara Khoury tells the consultant, "I lose because I'm just not a natural like the other girls. There's no point working on my serve." Her effort in practice has dropped noticeably since. Based on attribution theory, which goal should guide the consultant's plan?
options: Help her see the losses as reflecting her opponents' strength, so they feel less personal
Help her link the losses to changeable factors within her control, such as tactics and effort
Help her see the losses as reflecting temporary factors, such as an off day or unlucky net cords
Help her shift attention from match results to process goals for her serve in practice
rationales: Crediting opponents is an external attribution that may soften disappointment, but it gives her nothing she can act on and does not restore effort.

Zara attributes failure to an internal, stable, uncontrollable cause (lack of natural ability), the pattern Weiner's theory links to low expectations of success and reduced effort. Attribution retraining shifts explanations toward unstable, controllable causes such as tactics and effort, which sustain expectancy and motivation.

Temporary causes are unstable, which helps expectancy, but an off day and bad luck are still uncontrollable; they offer her no lever for practice, so they do less than controllable causes to restore effort.
Process goals are a useful technique, but they bypass the belief driving her withdrawal; while she thinks she lacks natural ability, she is unlikely to invest in serve practice.
takeaway: Attribution retraining moves failure explanations from stable, uncontrollable causes (ability) to unstable, controllable ones (effort, strategy).

stem: Elite figure skater Mei-Lin Zhou tells the consultant her confidence rises and falls with her coach's comments and with whether the judges seemed to like her last program. Asked what else she draws confidence from, she struggles to name anything. Drawing on Vealey's work on sources of sport confidence, which source should her plan develop first to make her confidence more stable?
options: Social support, by arranging more structured feedback from her coach before events
Demonstration of ability, by setting goals to outscore her main rivals this season
Physical self-presentation, by building pride in how she looks and moves on the ice
Mastery and preparation, by logging the skills she has improved and the work she has done
rationales: Social support is a recognized source of sport confidence, but she already leans on her coach's comments; adding more keeps her confidence dependent on others' evaluations, which is why it swings.
Demonstration of ability is a recognized source, but it rests on outperforming rivals, an outcome she does not control, so it would add another unstable foundation.
Physical self-presentation is a recognized source, but it centers on how she believes she looks to others, which is closely tied to the judges' evaluations that already destabilize her.

Vealey's multidimensional view of sport confidence identifies several sources, and those rooted in mastery and physical and mental preparation are more controllable and stable than others' evaluations. Developing these gives her confidence a foundation that day-to-day feedback cannot easily shake.
takeaway: Confidence that rests on controllable sources such as mastery and preparation is sturdier than confidence that depends on others' approval or outcomes.

stem: Masters swimmer Gloria Esposito logs her anxiety daily in the week before a national championship. Her worry ratings are high and fairly steady all week, while her ratings of butterflies and muscle tension stay low until the morning of the race and peak on the blocks. She says the shaky legs on the blocks make her starts sluggish. How should the consultant use this pattern in planning?
options: Start cognitive work early in the week, then add a somatic routine just before the start
Begin somatic techniques early in the week so her body stays calm as race day approaches
Concentrate cognitive and somatic work on race morning, when her ratings show the most change
Begin cognitive strategies early in the week, and continue the same strategies through the start
rationales: Multidimensional anxiety theory describes this temporal pattern: cognitive anxiety rises early and stays relatively high before competition, whereas somatic anxiety stays low until shortly before the event and peaks at the start. Matching technique to type and timing means addressing worry well before race day and adding somatic techniques for the pre-start window, where her shaky legs affect her starts.
Her bodily tension is low for most of the week, so week-long somatic work mismatches her data and leaves the high, steady worry untouched.

Race morning is when her somatic ratings change, but her worry has been high all week; waiting until then leaves the component the theory links most directly to poorer performance unaddressed for days.
Starting cognitive work early is right, but continuing only cognitive strategies leaves the somatic spike on the blocks, which she says slows her starts, without a matched somatic technique.
takeaway: Cognitive anxiety builds early and stays high; somatic anxiety spikes near the start, so time and match interventions to each component.

stem: Judoka Rafael Moreira, a national team member, recalls his best and worst matches. Before his best matches he felt tense, slightly irritated, and determined; before his worst he felt relaxed, content, and a little sluggish. He asks whether he should work on getting rid of the irritation. Consistent with the IZOF model, how should the consultant interpret this profile when planning?
options: As evidence that his best matches came at a moderate arousal level he should aim to maintain
As a sign that his irritation is a risk he should channel into calm, focused determination
As his individual optimal profile, which includes some unpleasant emotions that help him
As evidence that reading his tension as facilitative drives his success and should be reinforced
rationales: Framing the profile as a moderate-arousal sweet spot applies the inverted-U hypothesis; IZOF describes the specific emotions and intensities in his own zone rather than a universal moderate level.

Converting irritation into calm determination assumes unpleasant emotions are harmful, but his data link the calm, content state to his worst matches; removing the irritation could move him out of his zone.

Hanin's IZOF model holds that each athlete has an individual optimal emotional profile that can include unpleasant emotions that are functional for that athlete. His plan should help him reliably reach his own zone, not strip out emotions that help him.

Facilitative interpretation is the focus of Jones's directional perspective. It may be part of his experience, but his recall data describe the content and intensity of his emotions, which is what IZOF uses to define his zone.
takeaway: In IZOF, unpleasant emotions such as tension or irritation can be part of an athlete's optimal zone; don't assume they must be eliminated.

stem: Professional basketball point guard Ondine Caldwell is excellent at reading the defense and planning plays, but her coach notes that she keeps weighing options even after deciding to shoot, and her percentage on open shots has dropped. Using Nideffer's model of attention, which attentional shift should her plan target at the moment she releases the shot?
options: From broad-external to narrow-internal, to rehearse the feel of her shooting motion
From broad-internal to narrow-external, to fix her attention on the rim
From broad-internal to narrow-internal, to center herself with a single breath
From narrow-external to broad-external, to read the defenders' positions
rationales: Narrow-internal rehearsal suits preparation before a skill, not its execution; at release, attention on the feel of the motion competes with the external target.

Nideffer's model places attention on width and direction dimensions. Weighing options is broad-internal (analysis and planning), while executing a shot calls for a narrow-external focus on the target, so her plan should train a clean shift from analysis to the rim once she decides to shoot.
Centering is a useful narrow-internal step during a pause in play, but at the moment of release her attention needs to be on the target rather than on her breath.
Broad-external focus suits reading the defense before the decision, not executing the shot; widening attention at release adds cues that are no longer relevant.
takeaway: Nideffer: assess (broad-external), analyze (broad-internal), rehearse (narrow-internal), execute (narrow-external); performance suffers when an athlete is in the wrong quadrant for the moment.

stem: A youth wrestling club is moving four wrestlers up to a much tougher age division next season, where all four are expected to lose often at first. The consultant reviews their TEOSQ results and coach interviews to decide whose motivation to monitor most closely. According to achievement goal theory, which wrestler's profile suggests the greatest risk of withdrawing effort once the losses mount?
options: Malik: high task orientation, low ego orientation, moderate perceived ability
Ravi: high task orientation, high ego orientation, high perceived ability
Tobi: high task orientation, low ego orientation, low perceived ability
Sven: high ego orientation, low task orientation, high perceived ability
rationales: A strong task orientation defines success as personal improvement, which achievement goal theory links to sustained effort when results turn against an athlete.
High ego orientation carries some risk, but his equally high task orientation gives him a self-referenced way to feel successful when comparisons with opponents go badly.

Tobi's perceived ability is already low, but his strong task orientation means he judges success by his own improvement; achievement goal theory predicts that task-oriented athletes stay engaged even when they doubt their ability relative to others.

Nicholls's achievement goal theory predicts that ego orientation is adaptive only while perceived ability stays high. Sven defines success by beating others and has little task orientation to fall back on, so repeated losses are likely to erode his perceived ability and leave him at greatest risk of avoiding challenge and withdrawing effort.
takeaway: A high-ego, low-task athlete is protected only while perceived ability stays high; when losses erode it, effort withdrawal becomes likely.

stem: A consultant administers the Group Environment Questionnaire to a collegiate volleyball team whose coach reports poor in-game coordination. Scores are high on both social cohesion scales and on individual attractions to the group–task, but low on group integration–task. Which planning priority best fits these results?
options: Plan social events that help players connect with teammates outside their usual circles
Discuss with each player how to deepen their personal investment in their own role
Run team sessions in which players agree on shared match goals, roles, and standards
Re-administer the GEQ after several more matches before deciding where to intervene
rationales: Social cohesion is already high on both scales, so more social events target a strength and leave the task-integration gap untouched.

Individual attractions to the group–task, which reflect each player's personal involvement with the team's task, are already high; one-on-one work on personal investment addresses a dimension that is not the problem.

The GEQ separates individual attractions from group integration and task from social cohesion. Low group integration–task means players do not see the team as united around its task, so team building aimed at shared goals, clear roles, and agreed standards addresses that dimension directly.
The results already show a clear, interpretable pattern that matches the coach's report, so delaying planning to retest postpones help without adding needed information.
takeaway: Read GEQ results by scale: high social and individual task scores with low group integration–task call for group-level task team building (goals, roles, standards).

stem: A police academy asks a consultant to design a resilience program. Interviews show that many cadets view demanding training scenarios as threats they hope to avoid, and academy leaders are considering removing the most stressful scenarios. Based on Fletcher and Sarkar's grounded theory of psychological resilience, which program aim is most appropriate?
options: Build cadets’ confidence, focus, and peer support while they keep training in demanding scenarios
Screen incoming cadets with a resilience measure, and give extra support to those who score low
Teach arousal-control skills so cadets can keep their heart rates down during scenarios
Replace the most stressful scenarios with discussion-based case studies of real incidents
rationales: Fletcher and Sarkar found that psychological factors such as positive personality, motivation, confidence, focus, and perceived social support protect performers from the potential negative effects of stressors, partly by promoting challenge appraisals and helpful meta-cognitions. Building these factors while cadets keep engaging with demanding scenarios fits the model and helps shift their threat appraisals toward challenge.
Screening treats resilience mainly as something cadets bring with them, whereas the grounded theory frames it as a process shaped by modifiable psychological factors that every cadet can develop.
Arousal control can be one useful tool, but the model locates resilience mainly in psychological factors and how stressors are appraised, so a physiology-focused program misses the core mechanism.
Case studies are a sensible teaching method, but replacing the scenarios removes the engagement with stressors through which resilience develops and leaves cadets' threat appraisals unchallenged.
takeaway: Resilience develops through engagement with stressors, supported by psychological factors that promote challenge appraisals, not by removing adversity.

stem: Six weeks after an esports organization assembles a new five-player roster, the polite early scrims have given way to open arguments over shot-calling and who plays which role. The alarmed general manager asks whether the roster should be rebuilt. Using Tuckman's model of group development, how should the consultant interpret this situation and plan?
options: As a prolonged forming stage, with activities that invite players to get to know one another
As the storming stage, with sessions that help players agree on roles and shot-calling norms
As the norming stage, with sessions that reinforce the norms the players are developing
As a drop in social cohesion, with team-bonding activities held away from scrims
rationales: Forming is the polite, orienting phase the roster has already moved through; open conflict over roles signals the next stage, so get-to-know-you activities would not address it.

Tuckman's model describes forming (polite orientation), then storming (conflict over roles, influence, and direction), then norming and performing. Arguments over roles six weeks in fit storming, and helping the team agree on roles and norms supports the move to norming.
Norming follows storming, when members have begun to settle roles and expectations; this roster is still contesting them, so there are no stable norms yet to reinforce.
Social cohesion is a different framework, and the arguments center on task roles and decision-making rather than whether players like one another, so bonding activities would not resolve them.
takeaway: Conflict over roles after a polite start is Tuckman's storming stage; facilitate role clarity and norms rather than dismantling the group.

stem: Two paramedics, Oluwaseun and Bridget, work the same shifts with the same call volume, and both say the work matters deeply to them. Bridget describes busy nights as tough but manageable, citing her training and a supportive partner. Oluwaseun describes them as overwhelming and says he never knows whether he can handle the next call. Using Lazarus's transactional model of stress, which explanation should guide the consultant's plan for Oluwaseun?
options: A primary appraisal that busy nights put more at stake for him than for Bridget
Higher trait anxiety that leads him to read most calls as threatening
Physiological over-arousal during calls that crowds out clear decision-making
A secondary appraisal that his coping resources fall short of the demands
rationales: Primary appraisal concerns what is at stake, but both paramedics say the work matters deeply; the difference lies in whether he believes he can cope, not in how much the calls mean to him.

Trait anxiety is a person factor that can influence appraisal, but the transactional model focuses on the changeable appraisal of demands and resources, and his own words point to doubt about coping rather than a general disposition.

Over-arousal may be part of his stress response, but it is a consequence of the appraisal rather than the explanation the transactional model offers, and nothing in the stem describes impaired decisions on calls.

Lazarus's transactional model holds that stress arises from appraisal: primary appraisal of what is at stake and secondary appraisal of whether one's coping resources are adequate. Oluwaseun's doubt about handling the next call points to a secondary appraisal of insufficient resources, so the plan should build his coping resources and how he evaluates them.
takeaway: In the transactional model, stress depends on the appraised balance of demands and coping resources; doubt about coping signals a secondary-appraisal target.

stem: Conservatory pianist Anaya Deshpande is preparing for a high-pressure audition and asks the consultant to help her refine an imagery script. Her current script describes the hall, the piano, and the audience in vivid visual detail but says nothing about her own physical or emotional reactions. According to Lang's bioinformational theory, which revision would most strengthen the script?
options: Add response details, such as her quickened heartbeat and the feel of the keys under her fingers
Add the sounds, smells, and temperature of the hall so that every sense is engaged in the scene
Schedule the imagery at the audition's real time of day and run it at the length of her program
Switch to an external perspective so she can watch her posture and stage presence while she plays
rationales: Lang's bioinformational theory proposes that images contain stimulus propositions (features of the scene) and response propositions (the performer's physiological, behavioral, and emotional reactions), and that imagery has more impact when response propositions are included. Her script has only stimulus content, so adding her own responses is the key revision.
Multisensory detail makes the scene more vivid, but sounds, smells, and temperature are still stimulus propositions, the element the script already has in abundance.

Matching time of day and duration applies the timing and environment elements of the PETTLEP model. These are sensible refinements, but they do not add the response content that bioinformational theory identifies as missing.
Imagery perspective is a separate design choice; changing it does not supply response propositions, and an external view can make her bodily reactions less vivid.
takeaway: Bioinformational theory: imagery scripts work better when they include response propositions (what the performer feels and does), not just scene details.

stem: Survey and observation data from a youth gymnastics club show that gymnasts feel skilled and close to their teammates, but they report having no say in practice and rarely hearing why drills matter. Coaches give commands without explanation. Grounded in self-determination theory, which element should be central to the consultant's plan?
options: Coach training in giving specific, positive feedback on each gymnast's skill progress
Coach training in building warmth and personal connection with each gymnast
Coach training in explaining the purpose of drills and offering choices within limits
Coach training in setting clear, consistent rules and expectations for every practice
rationales: Informational feedback supports competence, a need the gymnasts already report as satisfied, so it does not address the gap the data reveal.
Warmth and connection support relatedness, which is already a strength for these gymnasts, so this training would not touch the unmet need.

Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic needs. Here autonomy is the unmet one, and autonomy-supportive coaching, such as giving rationales, offering choices within limits, and acknowledging athletes' perspectives, directly addresses it.

Clear structure complements autonomy support in SDT-based coaching, but these coaches already direct practice firmly; more rules without rationale or choice would not relieve the lack of voice the gymnasts describe.
takeaway: Match the intervention to the unmet SDT need; when autonomy is thwarted, train coaches in rationale-giving and choice within structure.

stem: A community aquatics program asks a consultant to help a group of 9- to 11-year-olds who are afraid to jump into the deep end. The children are not yet ready to attempt the jump themselves, but the instructor can show them one short demonstration, live or on video, first. Based on self-efficacy theory, which demonstration would most likely raise the children's efficacy?
options: A child their age who jumps in confidently and smoothly on the very first try
A slightly older child who calmly talks through each step aloud while jumping in
The instructor jumping in slowly while explaining exactly what to do at each step
A child their age who looks hesitant at first but then jumps in successfully
rationales: A same-age model is a good choice, but a model who shows no fear is a mastery model; fearful children identify less with someone who finds the task easy.
Narrating each step adds useful information, but an older child who stays calm throughout is less similar to these fearful learners than a same-age peer who copes with fear.
Instructor demonstrations convey technique well, but an adult expert is a dissimilar model, so the demonstration offers weaker evidence that the children themselves can do it.

Bandura's theory holds that vicarious experience raises efficacy most when observers see a model similar to themselves succeed. A same-age peer who shows initial hesitation and then copes successfully is a similar coping model, which is especially persuasive for fearful learners.
takeaway: Vicarious experience works best with similar models; a peer coping model is especially useful for fearful learners.

stem: Two distance runners, Kwabena and Anders, each narrowly miss qualifying for a national final. Kwabena tells the consultant, "I skipped too many tempo runs this block." Anders says, "I just don't have the build for this event." According to Weiner's attribution theory, which prediction should most influence the consultant's planning?
options: Kwabena is likelier to lose motivation, since his explanation is internal and self-critical
Anders is likelier to expect future failure, since his cause is stable and uncontrollable
Both face similar risk, since each explained the result with an internal cause
Anders is likelier to keep up his effort, since his cause spares him from self-blame
rationales: Kwabena's attribution is internal but unstable and controllable; Weiner's theory links that pattern to guilt and renewed effort, not lost motivation.

In Weiner's theory, the stability dimension drives expectations of future success, and controllability shapes emotions and effort. Anders's attribution to body build is stable and uncontrollable, predicting low expectancy and reduced motivation, so his explanation is the bigger planning concern.
Locus of causality is only one dimension; the runners differ on stability and controllability, which lead to very different predictions.
An uncontrollable cause may soften self-blame, but because it is also stable it predicts low expectancy of future success, which undermines rather than sustains effort.
takeaway: Stability predicts future expectancy and controllability predicts emotion and effort; internal-stable-uncontrollable attributions for failure are the most damaging.

stem: Collegiate diver Lachlan Reid and a teammate report similarly high pre-meet anxiety intensity. The teammate says a racing heart helps her feel sharp, while Lachlan says the same symptoms mean he is about to fall apart, and his scores suffer. Consistent with the directional perspective on competitive anxiety, which plan goal fits Lachlan best?
options: Help him interpret his symptoms as signs of readiness rather than signs of threat
Teach him somatic relaxation to bring his symptom intensity down before each dive
Give him a pre-dive cue that moves his attention from his sensations to his takeoff
Help him find the intensity linked to his best dives and aim for that personal zone
rationales: The directional perspective holds that performers can interpret the same anxiety intensity as facilitative or debilitative, and Hanton and Jones showed that cognitive skills can help athletes come to view their symptoms as facilitative. Since the teammate thrives at the same intensity, Lachlan's debilitative interpretation is the most useful target.

Lowering intensity can help some athletes, but the stem shows the same intensity accompanies his teammate's success, so intensity alone is not the core problem and his threat interpretation would remain.
A refocusing cue is a sound attentional tool, but it leaves his threat interpretation of the symptoms unchanged, which is the element the directional perspective targets.
Finding a personal optimal zone applies the IZOF model; it addresses intensity and emotion content rather than how he interprets the symptoms he has.
takeaway: When two performers share the same anxiety intensity but different outcomes, target the debilitative interpretation, not just the intensity.

stem: During a debrief after a training exercise, members of a police tactical team give conflicting accounts of who was responsible for clearing which room and which hand signal meant hold. All officers say they are committed to the team's mission and trust one another, and the same confusion appeared during a slow walk-through rehearsal. Each officer performs well individually, but the team's entry was slow and uncoordinated. Which concept best explains the breakdown and should guide the consultant's plan?
options: Low task cohesion, so the plan should build commitment to shared goals, norms, and standards
Social loafing, so the plan should make each officer's contribution identifiable
Weak shared mental models, so the plan should align roles, signals, and sequences
Attentional narrowing under stress, so the plan should add graded stress exposure
rationales: Task cohesion concerns commitment to shared goals, and the officers report strong commitment; their problem is inconsistent understanding of who does what, not a lack of unity.
Social loafing is reduced effort in a group, but these officers are trying hard; they are simply working from different assumptions.

Shared mental models are team members' overlapping knowledge of roles, cues, and procedures that lets them anticipate one another and coordinate. Conflicting beliefs about responsibilities and signals indicate weak shared mental models, so pre-briefs, rehearsal, and structured debriefs that align that knowledge are the right focus.
Stress-related narrowing could affect a high-stakes entry, but the same confusion appeared in a slow, low-stress walk-through, which points to a knowledge problem rather than an arousal problem.
takeaway: Good individuals who coordinate poorly often lack shared mental models; build common knowledge of roles, cues, and sequences.

stem: Professional tennis player Sofia Lindqvist had worried all week about her ranking. Leading 5–1 in the first set, she suddenly lost five straight games. At the changeover she took two slow breaths, then lost the next game as well. Reviewing the match with her afterward, which changeover plan best reflects the catastrophe model?
options: A brief psych-up routine to lift her intensity back to the level she had while leading
A short breathing routine to bring her arousal back to its level before the slide
A longer reset that drops arousal well below its pre-slide level and settles her worry first
A reappraisal cue so she reads her racing heart and tight arms as signs of readiness
rationales: With cognitive anxiety high, more physiological arousal pushes her further past the catastrophe threshold, so psyching up would worsen the problem rather than restore her earlier play.

Returning arousal to its pre-collapse level assumes performance retraces its path, but the catastrophe model predicts hysteresis: after a collapse, a small reduction in arousal does not restore performance, which fits what happened after her two breaths.

Hardy's catastrophe model holds that under high cognitive anxiety, rising arousal can trigger a sudden drop, and because of hysteresis recovery is not a simple reversal. She needs to bring arousal well below the level at which she collapsed and reduce her cognitive anxiety before rebuilding toward her optimal state.

Reappraising symptoms as readiness applies the directional perspective; it changes interpretation but leaves both her high worry and her elevated arousal in place, which the catastrophe model says must come down after a collapse.
takeaway: After a catastrophe-style collapse, small calming steps won't restore play (hysteresis); substantial arousal reduction plus lower worry comes first.

stem: A consultant runs weekly mental skills sessions with a collegiate soccer team. So far the consultant has lectured, assigned mandatory worksheets, and reminded players that the coach will check completion. Players say the skills make sense and they enjoy one another's company, but they call the sessions "homework for the coach," and few report using the skills on the field. Which adjustment is most consistent with self-determination theory?
options: Invite players to choose which skills to work on and explain how each links to their goals
Add short in-session drills so players experience early success with each new skill
Pair players as partners who check in with each other on skill use each week
Shorten the lectures and add small-group role-plays of each skill in match situations
rationales: Self-determination theory predicts that controlling delivery yields compliance without internalization. Offering meaningful choice and a clear rationale supports autonomy, the need the players' "homework for the coach" comments show is being thwarted, which promotes more self-determined engagement and use of the skills outside sessions.
Early success supports competence, but players already say the skills make sense; the drills leave the mandatory, coach-checked structure that is undermining their ownership in place.
Peer check-ins draw on relatedness, which is already strong, and adding another layer of monitoring may feel like more accountability rather than more choice.
Active practice is good teaching, but it changes the format without changing who decides; the sessions would still feel like required work done for the coach.
takeaway: Compliance without engagement signals a controlling climate; SDT points to choice and rationale, not more structure, drills, or monitoring.

stem: During scenario-based training, police recruits face a simulated armed suspect. In the highest-stress version, recruit Dana Kowalczyk locks onto the suspect's weapon and fails to notice a second person entering from the side, a cue she catches easily in calmer versions. Based on cue utilization theory, which explanation and training adjustment best fit her performance?
options: Low arousal left her attention broad and unfocused, so add an activation routine before entry
Her scanning is not yet automatic, so add more scanning repetitions in calm, low-stress versions
Worry about being evaluated used up her attention, so add a routine to quiet her self-talk
High arousal narrowed her attention past relevant cues, so train scanning under graded stress
rationales: The miss happens only in the highest-stress version and she fixates on one cue rather than drifting, which points to arousal that is too high and attention that is too narrow, not the reverse.
She already detects the second person easily in calmer versions, so the skill exists; more low-stress repetitions would not prepare her for the arousal level at which the cue drops out.

Worry consuming attentional resources reflects processing-efficiency accounts rather than cue utilization theory, and her fixation on the weapon describes narrowed attention rather than attention pulled inward.

Easterbrook's cue utilization theory holds that rising arousal narrows attention, first screening out irrelevant cues and then, at high levels, relevant ones. Losing a peripheral threat only under peak stress fits that pattern, so training should build arousal regulation and practice scanning under gradually increasing stress.
takeaway: Missing relevant cues only under peak stress signals arousal-driven attentional narrowing; train arousal control and scanning under graded stress.

stem: A consultant observes a youth basketball coach who posts a ranked list of players' free-throw percentages, directs most praise to the top shooters, and groups players by ability for drills. Several lower-ranked players have stopped trying hard in practice. In coaching the coach, which change is most consistent with creating a task-involving motivational climate?
options: Keep the ranked list but add a weekly award for the most improved shooter
Replace the rankings with recognition of each player's own improvement and effort
Form mixed-ability pairs and post weekly rankings of each pair's combined percentage
Give lower-ranked players extra coaching so they can close the gap on the top shooters
rationales: A most-improved award adds some recognition of progress, but keeping the public ranking leaves normative comparison at the center of the climate, and only one player is recognized each week.

Achievement goal theory distinguishes task-involving (mastery) climates, which define success as personal improvement and effort, from ego-involving climates built on comparison. Shifting recognition to self-referenced progress and effort is the core of mastery-climate coach training and supports continued effort from all players.
Mixed-ability pairs add cooperation, but ranking the pairs keeps success defined by outperforming others, so the climate remains ego-involving.
Extra coaching is well-meant, but framing its purpose as catching the top shooters still defines success by comparison, and singling out the lowest-ranked players can signal low ability.
takeaway: A task-involving climate recognizes individual improvement and effort; public rankings and comparison-based goals, even well-meant ones, create ego-involving climates.

stem: Renée Dubois, 52, joined a supervised exercise program six weeks ago after medical clearance. She tells the consultant she is thinking of quitting because heavy breathing and sore legs during sessions prove her body just can't do this anymore, even though she has completed every workout. Based on self-efficacy theory, which adjustment most directly targets the source of information that is lowering her efficacy?
options: Ask the instructor to point out her progress and praise her effort during each session
Pair her with a member her age who struggled early on but now trains comfortably
Suggest that the instructor ease her session intensity until the breathlessness fades
Help her reinterpret breathlessness and soreness as normal signs that she is adapting
rationales: Credible praise is verbal persuasion, a weaker source that is unlikely to outweigh the bodily evidence she believes she is getting in every session.

A similar coping model is a strong form of vicarious experience, but it adds a different source of information while leaving her misreading of her own sensations, the source driving her doubt, unchanged.
Easing intensity is a training decision for the exercise staff, and reducing the sensations without changing how she reads them may confirm her belief that her body cannot handle the work.

Bandura lists physiological and emotional states as a source of efficacy information; what matters is how people interpret them. Renée reads normal exertion as incapacity, so reframing those signals, alongside highlighting that she has completed every workout, addresses the source lowering her efficacy.
takeaway: Bodily sensations influence efficacy through their interpretation; reframe normal exertion signals rather than adding persuasion or reducing the work.

stem: A fitness center asks a consultant to help instructors improve attendance in a 10-week group exercise class for adults. Members rarely talk to one another, and many stop coming by the fourth week. Drawing on Carron and Spink's team-building approach for exercise groups, which strategy should the consultant coach the instructors to deliver?
options: Send each member personalized reminder messages, and track attendance privately
Give the class a group name, shared norms, and regular partner work in each session
Run a goal-setting session in which each member sets a personal attendance target
Match each member with an exercise buddy to train with between class sessions
rationales: Reminders and private tracking are reasonable individual adherence tools, but they treat members as separate exercisers and do nothing to build the group cohesion the team-building approach targets.

Carron and Spink's team-building protocol for exercise classes targets cohesion through group distinctiveness (such as a class name), group norms, and interaction and communication among members. Greater cohesion in exercise groups is associated with better attendance and lower dropout.
Personal attendance targets apply goal-setting at the individual level; they may help some members, but they do not create the shared identity and interaction that build class cohesion.
Exercise buddies add social support, but they operate outside the class and in pairs, so they do not build the class-level distinctiveness, norms, and interaction that the protocol uses.
takeaway: In exercise groups, team building that creates distinctiveness, norms, and member interaction builds cohesion, which supports adherence.

stem: Before a championship game, a consultant leads a collegiate field hockey team through a group relaxation script. Afterward, forward Nia Achterberg says she feels flat. Her performance history shows she plays best when she feels highly energized and a bit on edge. Consistent with the IZOF model, what adjustment should the consultant make for Nia?
options: Give her a short energizing routine to lift her intensity back into her zone
Help her reappraise the flat feeling as calm readiness rather than a problem
Keep her in the group script and add a confidence-building self-talk cue
Shift the whole team's pre-game routine from relaxation to a group psych-up
rationales: IZOF holds that optimal emotional intensity is individual and can be high. Nia's history places her zone at high intensity, so after relaxation drops her below it, she needs energizing strategies to move back into her zone.
Reappraisal applies the directional perspective, but her history shows she plays best when highly energized; relabeling a low-intensity state does not move her back into that zone.
Self-talk can support confidence, but staying in the relaxation script keeps lowering the intensity that her best performances require.

A team-wide psych-up applies a group fix to an individual need; teammates whose zones sit at lower intensity could be pushed out of theirs, which contradicts IZOF's emphasis on individual differences.
takeaway: Group preparation should allow individual adjustment; an athlete with a high-intensity optimal zone may need energizing, not relaxation.

stem: A company's virtual wellness challenge awarded points and gift cards for logging walks. Employees who enjoyed walking before the challenge now say walking feels like a chore they do for points, and once the rewards ended their activity fell below what it had been beforehand. As the consultant helps redesign the program, which explanation and adjustment best fit self-determination theory?
options: The challenge lacked social connection, so add team-based walking groups with shared goals
The targets were too vague, so set specific weekly step goals with progress feedback
The rewards stopped too abruptly, so taper them gradually over several weeks instead
The rewards felt controlling, so emphasize choice and personal reasons for walking
rationales: Relatedness is a basic need and walking groups could help, but employees' comments that walking became a chore done for points point to the rewards themselves, not a lack of connection.
Specific goals with feedback apply goal-setting theory and can raise activity, but they do not explain why people who already enjoyed walking lost interest once rewards were introduced.
Tapering treats the problem as the rewards' removal, but the loss of enjoyment began while the rewards were in place, which points to how the rewards were experienced.

Cognitive evaluation theory, part of self-determination theory, predicts that expected tangible rewards experienced as controlling can undermine intrinsic motivation, leaving people less engaged once rewards stop. Redesigning around autonomy, with choice and personally meaningful reasons, supports more self-determined activity.
takeaway: Expected, controlling rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (cognitive evaluation theory); design for autonomy instead.

stem: Late in a lopsided game, collegiate center fielder Mateo Ruiz finds himself noticing crowd chatter, the scoreboard, and teammates' banter, and he is slow to react when a fly ball heads his way. In close games he is sharp and quick off the mark. Based on cue utilization theory, which adjustment should the consultant help him use in low-stakes moments?
options: A slow calming breath before each pitch to steady his body and clear his head
A brief activation routine before each pitch to raise arousal and sharpen his focus
A cue to stay broad-external so he keeps tracking the runners and game situation
A quick mental rehearsal of his first step on balls hit to either side of him
rationales: Calming breaths lower arousal, but his arousal is already low in blowouts; lowering it further would keep his attention broad and prolong the problem.

Cue utilization theory holds that at low arousal attention is broad and takes in irrelevant cues, while a moderate rise narrows attention so irrelevant cues drop out. A brief activation routine before each pitch raises arousal toward his optimal level and refocuses him on relevant cues such as the batter and the ball.
Situational awareness matters for a fielder, but his attention is already too broad; a cue to stay broad does not screen out the crowd and scoreboard that are crowding in.
Imagery of his first step is a reasonable preparation tool, but it does not raise his low arousal, and rehearsing internally between pitches can pull attention further from the batter.
takeaway: Cue utilization works both ways: too little arousal leaves attention too broad, so a modest activation boost can screen out irrelevant cues.

stem: After a narrow loss, players on a professional rugby team spend the debrief blaming the referee and the weather. The head coach asks the consultant to help run the next debrief. Based on attribution theory, which adjustment is most likely to support players' motivation going forward?
options: Guide players to identify causes they can control, such as defensive structure and effort
Acknowledge the referee's calls briefly, then move the debrief on to next week's game plan
Guide players to identify causes that were temporary, such as the wet conditions on the day
Guide players to credit the opponent's quality, so the loss is not taken as a judgment on them
rationales: Weiner's attribution theory links controllable and unstable attributions for failure to sustained expectancy and effort. Steering the debrief toward factors the team controls and can change, such as structure, decisions, and effort, gives players something to act on.
Moving on quickly avoids dwelling on the referee, but it leaves the external, uncontrollable explanation unchallenged and misses the debrief's chance to shape how players explain the loss.
Temporary causes are unstable, which helps expectancy, but weather is uncontrollable; players leave with nothing they can change, so effort is less likely to rise.
Crediting the opponent is external and may protect self-esteem, but it is uncontrollable and, if seen as lasting, stable, which is linked to lowered expectations rather than renewed effort.
takeaway: In debriefs, guide attributions for losses toward controllable, changeable causes to sustain expectancy and effort.

stem: First-year collegiate gymnast Yolanda Pires is learning a new release move on the uneven bars. In closed practices she now lands it about half the time, but when teammates and parents watch open practices her attempts fall apart. The team's veterans, by contrast, say they hit their best routines in front of a crowd. Based on Zajonc's social facilitation theory, which practice-scheduling change should the consultant suggest to her coach?
options: Schedule most of her attempts during open practices so that being watched becomes routine
Have teammates watch and cheer each attempt in closed sessions to build supportive pressure
Keep early attempts in closed sessions, then add observers once she lands it consistently
Have a veteran perform the move first, then let her attempt it while the veteran watches
rationales: Getting used to observers is a reasonable later goal, but social facilitation theory predicts that an audience raises arousal and strengthens the dominant response; for a half-learned skill that response is still often an error, so frequent watched attempts now would mostly rehearse failure.
Supportive teammates are still an audience; bringing them into closed sessions adds the same arousal effect at the stage when the move is least well learned.

Zajonc's social facilitation theory holds that the presence of others increases arousal, which helps performance when the dominant response is correct (well-learned skills, as for the veterans) and hurts it when the skill is new. Learning the move away from observers until it is consistent, then adding observers gradually, fits that prediction.

Watching a skilled teammate offers useful vicarious information, but having the veteran watch each attempt adds an observer while the move is still unreliable, which is the condition the theory predicts will impair her.
takeaway: Audiences help well-learned skills and hurt new ones (social facilitation); learn new skills without observers, then add them as the skill becomes dominant.

stem: Startup founder Priscila Navarro has an investor pitch in two weeks. She tells the consultant, "I know how big this meeting is, and I'm fine presenting the product, but if they ask about our financials I won't know what to say." Using Lazarus's model of stress appraisal, which focus for the next session best targets her secondary appraisal?
options: Explore how much this single meeting will really decide the company's future
Teach her a breathing routine to manage nerves in the opening minutes of the pitch
Rehearse the product demo until her delivery feels smooth and automatic
Identify the questions she dreads and build resources, such as prepared answers
rationales: Reconsidering how much the meeting matters targets primary appraisal (what is at stake), not her judgment about whether she can cope, and minimizing a genuinely important meeting is unlikely to be credible.
Breathing is an emotion-focused tool that manages the stress response; it does not change her evaluation of whether she has what she needs to handle the questions.
Polishing the demo builds resources for the part of the pitch she already feels able to handle, leaving the area where she doubts her coping untouched.

In Lazarus's model, secondary appraisal is the evaluation of one's coping resources and options. Her worry centers on not being able to answer certain questions, so identifying them and strengthening her resources for that challenge targets secondary appraisal directly.
takeaway: Primary appraisal asks what is at stake; secondary appraisal asks whether I can cope, so strengthen resources where the doubt lies.

stem: During tournament matches, esports player Jae-won Park keeps analyzing a mistake from earlier rounds and misses information about enemy rotations around the map. In practice debriefs, he can describe exactly what he should have noticed. Using Nideffer's model of attention, which refocusing cue should the consultant help him build into his in-game routine?
options: A cue to shift from broad-internal to narrow-external focus, fixing on his crosshair placement
A cue to shift from broad-internal to narrow-internal focus, rehearsing his next ability sequence
A cue to shift from broad-internal to broad-external focus, scanning enemy positions
A cue to shift from narrow-external to broad-internal focus, re-planning his strategy for the round
rationales: A narrow-external focus on aim suits the moment of execution, but it would still miss the wide-ranging information about enemy movement he needs.
Narrow-internal rehearsal keeps his attention inside his head, which is where it is already stuck, so external information would still be missed.

Nideffer's model describes attention on width and direction dimensions. Analyzing an earlier mistake is a broad-internal focus, while tracking enemy movement across the map requires broad-external attention, so a cue that ends the analysis and returns him to broad-external scanning matches the demands of the moment.
Broad-internal planning is the kind of analysis already pulling him away from the game; it belongs between rounds or in the debrief, not during play.
takeaway: When an athlete is stuck in internal analysis and missing environmental information, a refocusing cue should shift attention to broad-external.

stem: Coaches at a youth soccer academy, worried about players' well-being, have dropped competitive selection matches, stopped giving critical feedback, and step in whenever a drill becomes frustrating. Players completed a coping-skills workshop in the autumn, yet they now struggle badly when they face setbacks at tournaments. Drawing on resilience research in sport, which adjustment should the consultant recommend to the coaches?
options: Reintroduce selection matches and honest feedback, and debrief setbacks with players afterward
Keep the low-pressure environment, and add a peer-mentor scheme for support at tournaments
Reintroduce selection matches and blunt feedback, and step back so players learn to self-regulate
Run a refresher coping-skills workshop, then reintroduce selection matches next season
rationales: Resilience research in sport, including Fletcher and Sarkar's work, indicates that resilience develops when performers engage with manageable stressors while feeling supported. Reintroducing appropriate challenge and honest feedback, with coaches helping players make sense of setbacks, creates that high-challenge, high-support environment.
Peer mentors add support, but keeping the environment low in challenge extends the overprotection that left players unprepared; support without challenge does not build resilience.

Restoring challenge is right, but pairing it with blunt feedback and withdrawn support risks overwhelming adolescents; resilience research pairs high challenge with high support rather than trading one for the other.
Players have already had coping-skills training without transfer; postponing challenge for another season delays the engagement with stressors through which those skills become resilience.
takeaway: Resilience grows from manageable challenge paired with support; removing adversity or removing support both undermine it.

stem: During the off-season, a consultant holds weekly group video calls with para swimmers who train alone in different cities. Each swimmer designs their own sessions and is hitting their split targets, but several describe the calls as "reporting to a spreadsheet" and say they miss training alongside others. Motivation is slipping. Which adjustment is most consistent with self-determination theory?
options: Let the swimmers set the agenda for each call and choose which metrics to discuss
Give each swimmer more detailed feedback on progress toward their split targets
Add a weekly group challenge that awards points for every session a swimmer logs
Build in time for the swimmers to share experiences and encourage one another
rationales: More say over the agenda supports autonomy, but the swimmers already design their own training; the need going unmet is connection, not choice.
Detailed feedback supports competence, which their split results suggest is already satisfied, and it keeps the calls centered on numbers rather than people.
A points challenge adds a group element, but it rewards logging with points, an external contingency that can feel controlling and still treats the calls as reporting.

Self-determination theory identifies relatedness, feeling connected to and cared for by others, as a basic need alongside autonomy and competence. These swimmers show satisfied autonomy and competence but miss connection, so peer sharing and mutual support target the unmet need.
takeaway: Diagnose which SDT need is unmet; for isolated remote athletes, build connection rather than more data, choice, or points.

stem: Three weeks before a world championship, a minor illness cost alpine skier Lukas Brenner a week of training. In a session he says his confidence has disappeared because the work isn't there anymore. Drawing on Vealey's sport-confidence research, which approach should the consultant take to address the source of his doubt?
options: Have him image flawless runs on the championship course each day this week
Review his training log and results to reconnect him with evidence of his preparation
Point out that several of his rivals have also battled illness and setbacks this season
Shift his focus to process cues for each section of the course on race day
rationales: Mastery imagery can support confidence, but it does not answer his specific doubt, which is that his preparation is lacking; imagined runs are not evidence of the work he believes is missing.

Vealey's research identifies physical and mental preparation and mastery as key sources of sport confidence. Lukas is discounting a season of preparation because of one missed week, so reviewing concrete evidence of his training and accomplishments rebuilds confidence from sources he controls.
Rivals' setbacks reflect situational factors he does not control, so confidence built on them is fragile and turns attention away from his own preparation.
Process cues are useful for race-day focus, but they leave his belief that his preparation is inadequate untouched, which is the source of his lost confidence.
takeaway: Rebuild shaken sport confidence from the source the athlete doubts, often evidence of preparation and mastery.

stem: Midway through a training block, junior track cyclist Ayesha Rahman's coach keeps telling her to just do her best in each session, and her effort varies widely from day to day. The consultant is helping the coach refine the goal-setting process. According to Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory, which adjustment is most likely to improve her effort and persistence?
options: Keep the do-your-best instructions, and add detailed feedback after each session
Set specific, challenging targets for each session and review her progress against them
Set specific session targets she can comfortably reach, to build her early commitment
Set a specific, challenging goal for the season, and review her progress toward it monthly
rationales: Feedback helps most when it can be compared with a goal; without a specific standard, do-your-best instructions still leave her effort without clear direction.

Goal-setting theory holds that specific, difficult goals with feedback outperform vague do-your-best goals because they direct attention, mobilize effort, increase persistence, and prompt strategy development. Concrete session targets with progress feedback address her inconsistent effort directly.

Specificity helps, but the theory links goal difficulty to effort: easy targets demand little and so mobilize little, whereas harder goals, given commitment and ability, produce more effort and persistence.
A season goal is specific and challenging, but it is distant and reviewed rarely, so it gives little direction or feedback for effort in day-to-day sessions; proximal session goals do that work.
takeaway: Specific, challenging goals with frequent feedback beat do-your-best goals by directing attention, effort, persistence, and strategy.

stem: A consultant has been teaching progressive muscle relaxation to amateur triathlete Minh Tran, whose CSAI-2 and interview data show high cognitive anxiety and low somatic anxiety. After three weeks of practice, Minh says his body feels relaxed but he still cannot stop worrying about the race. Which adjustment best reflects the matching principle for anxiety interventions?
options: Shift to cognitive strategies, such as restructuring worries and refocusing attention
Switch to diaphragmatic breathing, which works faster than muscle relaxation on race day
Add a pre-race psych-up routine with energizing self-talk to raise his activation
Add heart-rate biofeedback so he can confirm that his body is relaxed before races
rationales: Multidimensional anxiety theory separates cognitive and somatic anxiety, and the matching hypothesis proposes that interventions work best when they target the type of anxiety a person experiences. Minh's problem is worry, so cognitive strategies fit better than more somatic relaxation.
Diaphragmatic breathing may be quicker to use, but it is another somatic technique aimed at bodily tension, which is already low.
Energizing self-talk raises activation, but his difficulty is worry rather than low arousal, so a psych-up routine addresses neither the type nor the direction of his problem.
Biofeedback that confirms bodily relaxation is another somatic tool aimed at the component that is already low, and it leaves his worry untouched.
takeaway: Match the technique to the anxiety: cognitive strategies for worry, somatic techniques for bodily tension.

stem: Players on a professional ice hockey team each report confidence in their own skills, but in interviews several say the team always falls apart on the penalty kill. Their penalty-kill success rate has dropped across the season. Based on Bandura's concept of collective efficacy, which adjustment should the consultant and coaching staff make to practices?
options: Have each player set individual skill goals for their own penalty-kill duties
Build penalty-kill drills the unit can succeed at together, then raise the difficulty
Show video of a similar-level team that turned its penalty kill around midseason
Have the coaches walk through why the system is sound, then voice belief in the unit
rationales: Individual goals target personal efficacy, which is already high; the doubt is about how the unit performs together.

Collective efficacy is a group's shared belief in its combined capability to perform a task. Like individual self-efficacy, it is built most powerfully through mastery experiences, so graded drills in which the penalty-kill unit succeeds together give the group direct evidence of its joint capability.
A similar team is a well-chosen vicarious source, but vicarious experience is generally weaker than the group's own success, especially after a season of repeated breakdowns.
A reasoned explanation from credible coaches is the strongest form of verbal persuasion, but persuasion is still a weaker source that is unlikely to outweigh the unit's own experience of failure.
takeaway: Confident individuals can still doubt the team; build collective efficacy through shared, graded mastery experiences.

stem: A regional theatre company's cast has worked closely together for a five-month production run that ends next week. Several actors say they feel unsettled and unsure how to say goodbye, and the director asks the consultant to help the cast as a group during the final days. Using the expanded version of Tuckman's model of group development, which approach best fits this stage?
options: Run role-clarification exercises so the cast finishes the run without friction
Hold a goal-setting session to keep standards high through the final week of performances
Facilitate a closing session to reflect on contributions and plan for what comes next
Offer individual sessions to any actor who wants help with feelings about the ending
rationales: Role-clarification work fits the storming stage; the cast's concern now is the group's ending, not conflict over roles.
Goal-setting supports the performing stage, but the actors' unsettled feelings are about the group ending, which performance goals do not address.

The adjourning stage, added in a later revision of Tuckman's model, describes a group disbanding after completing its task, often with mixed feelings. A structured closing that acknowledges contributions and helps members prepare for what comes next addresses that stage directly.
Individual sessions may help a few actors, but the director asked for help with the cast as a group, and adjourning is a group-level process best addressed together.
takeaway: When a group is ending (adjourning), facilitate closure: reflect on contributions and prepare members for transition.
